edition.locus: Adversus Marcionem 3.11 (putatiua caro / natiuitas / Christus creatoris)

source_text: Totas istas praestigias putatiuae in Christo corpulentiae Marcion illa intentione suscepit, ne ex testimonio substantiae humanae natiuitas quoque eius defenderetur atque ita Christus creatoris uindicaretur, ut qui nascibilis ac per hoc carneus adnuntiaretur. stultissime et hic Ponticus: quasi non facilius crederetur in deo caro non nata quam falsa, praestruentibus uel maxime fidem istam angelis creatoris in carne uera conuersatis nec tamen nata. nam et Philumene illa magis persuasit Appelli ceterisque desertoribus Marcionis ex fide quidem Christum circumtulisse carnem, nullius tamen natiuitatis, utpote de elementis eam mutuatum. quodsi uerebatur Marcion, ne fides carnis natiuitatis quoque fidem induceret, sine dubio qui homo uidebatur natus utique credebatur. nam et mulier quaedam exclamauerat: beatus uenter, qui te portauit, et ubera, quae hausisti. et quomodo mater et fratres eius dicti sunt foris stare? certe, cum et ipse se filium hominis praedicaret, natum scilicet profitebatur. et uidebimus de his capitulis suo in tempore: nunc, ut haec omnia ad euangelii distulerim examinationem, tamen quod supra statui: si omni modo natus credi habebat qui homo uidebatur, uane natiuitatis fidem consilio imaginariae carnis expugnandam putauit. quid enim profuit non uere fuisse quod pro uero haberetur. tam carnem quam natiuitatem? aut si dixeris: uiderit opinio humana, iam deum tuum honoras fallaciae titulo, si aliud se sciebat esse quam quod homines fecerat opinari, iam tu potuisti etiam natiuitatem putatiuam illi accommodasse, ne in hanc quoque impegisses quaestionem. nam et mulierculae nonnumquam praegnantes sibi uidentur, aut sanguinis tributo aut aliqua ualitudine inflatae. et utique debuerat phantasmati? scaenam decucurrisse, ne originem carnis non desaltasset qui personam substantiae ipsius egisset. plane natiuitatis mendacium recusasti: ipsam enim carnem ueram edidisti. turpissimum scilicet dei etiam uera natiuitas. age iam, perora in illa sanctissima et reuerenda opera naturae, inuehere in totum quod es; carnis atque animae originem destrue; cloacam uoca uterum, tanti animalis, id est hominis, producendi officinam: persequere et partus inmunda et pudenda tormenta et ipsius exinde puerperii spurcos anxios ludicros exitus: tamen, cum omnia ista destruxeris, ut deo indigna confirmes, non erit indignior morte natiuitas et cruce infantia et natura poena et caro damnatione. si uere ista passus est Christus. minus fuit nasci; si mendacio passus est, ut phantasma, potuit: et mendacio nasci. summa ista Marcionis argumenta. per quae alium efficit Christum, satis, opinor, ostendimus non consistere omnino, dum docemus magis utique competere deo ueritatem quam mendacium eius habitus, in quo Christum suum exhibuit. si ueritas fuit, caro fuit, si caro fuit, natus est. ea enim, quae expugnat haec haeresis, confirmantur, cum ea, per quae expugnat, destruuntur. itaque, si carneus habebitur, quia natus, et natus, quia carneus, quia phantasma non fuerit, ipse erit agnoscendus, qui in carne et ex natiuitate uenturus adnuntiabatur a creatoris prophetis. utpote Christus creatoris.
pass_a_gloss: Marcion’s putative body blocks nativity→Creator’s Christ; birth no worse than death/cross; if true habit then flesh then born — the prophesied Creator Christ.
pass_b_english: Marcion took up all these tricks of putative bulk in Christ with this aim: that from the witness of human substance his nativity too should not be defended, and so Christ should be claimed as the Creator’s — as one announced birth-able and therefore fleshy. Most stupidly here too the Pontic: as if flesh not born would not be believed in God more easily than false flesh, while the Creator’s angels who lived in true flesh yet were not born prepare that faith most of all. For that Philumene more persuaded Apelles and the other deserters of Marcion that Christ did indeed carry flesh in faith, yet of no nativity, borrowing it from the elements. But if Marcion feared that faith in flesh would also bring in faith in nativity, without doubt the one who seemed man was believed born. For a certain woman had also cried out: Blessed the womb that bore you, and the breasts you drank. And how were his mother and brothers said to stand outside? Certainly, when he himself also preached himself Son of man, he was confessing that he was born. We will look at these chapters in their time; now, though I have put all this off to examination of the gospel, still what I set above: if the one who seemed man had to be believed born in every way, he thought vainly that faith in nativity was to be stormed by a plan of imaginary flesh. For what did it profit that what was held for true was not truly so — flesh as much as nativity? Or if you say, Let human opinion see to itself — already you honor your god with the title of deceit, if he knew himself to be other than what he had made men think; already you could have fitted even a putative nativity to him, so as not to strike on this question too. For little women sometimes seem pregnant to themselves, swollen by a tribute of blood or by some illness. And surely a phantasm ought to have run through the stage-play, lest he who played the role of the substance itself should not have danced out the origin of flesh. Clearly you refused the lie of nativity: for you put forth the flesh itself as true. Most shameful, of course, even a true nativity of God. Come then, speechify against those most holy and reverend works of nature; inveigh against the whole of what you are; destroy the origin of flesh and soul; call the womb a sewer, the workshop of producing so great an animal — that is, man; chase the unclean and shameful torments of birth and then the foul, anxious, laughable exits of the lying-in itself: yet when you have destroyed all that to confirm them unworthy of God, nativity will not be more unworthy than death, infancy than the cross, nature than punishment, flesh than damnation. If Christ truly suffered these things, it was less to be born; if he suffered by a lie, as a phantasm, he could also be born by a lie. These are Marcion’s chief arguments by which he makes another Christ; we have shown, I think, that they do not stand at all, while we teach that truth of that habit in which he exhibited his Christ fits God more than a lie. If it was truth, it was flesh; if it was flesh, he was born. For what this heresy storms are confirmed when what it storms with are destroyed. Therefore if he will be held fleshy because born, and born because fleshy, because he was not a phantasm, he himself must be recognized who was announced by the Creator’s prophets as about to come in flesh and from nativity — as the Creator’s Christ.

lemmas.lat: si ueritas fuit, caro fuit, si caro fuit, natus est
lemmas.sense: if truth, flesh; if flesh, born

choices.why: putatiua corpulentia is polemical ‘as-if’ substance, not mild appearance.
nascibilis…carneus keeps Tertullian’s birth→flesh chain without later system words.
Christus creatoris is Tertullian’s own contrast term.

notes: Incarnation/nativity locus beyond 2.5; natiuitas paired with cross/death unworthiness reductio.
